scenes.title: Lab Preparation: Strands, AgentCore and Agent Squad
scenes.narration: We are about to build a small agent-routing lab, and this slide gives the preparation checklist. The first panel prepares a supported Python environment, preferably a virtual environment with an appropriate version. The second panel configures AWS CLI credentials and confirms the account and Region. Third, verify access to the Amazon Bedrock model that will power the agent. Fourth, install the required dependencies such as Strands and the AgentCore tooling, checking that the versions are compatible. The fifth panel plans cleanup before any deployment begins. Look at the lab lifecycle across the middle: prepare, build, test, deploy, verify and tear down. Those are not interchangeable steps. Validate the agent locally before deploying, and inspect the deployed resources afterward so the final state matches the intended architecture. The orange warning along the bottom reminds us to remove any AWS resources created for the lab when we are finished. This avoids lingering cost and reduces the exposure of unnecessary test infrastructure.

scenes.title: Lab Architecture: Route to the Right Agent
scenes.narration: This slide shows the target lab architecture. The user asks a question about how many keywords appear in a phrase. The request reaches Agent Squad, which uses intent classification to choose an appropriate specialist. General questions can go directly to an Amazon Bedrock foundation model, but questions involving mathematics, time or counting are routed to a Strands agent with tools. Follow the orange path toward the Strands agent on the right. It has a calculator, clock and count-keywords tool available. The selected tool performs the task and the agent returns the answer. A dashed optional branch shows how the Strands agent can later run in AgentCore Runtime rather than only in a local process. The key learning outcome is not the exact keyword count. It is separating classification, specialist routing, authorized tool execution and the final answer. When testing, include ambiguous requests and verify that the router doesn't send every question to the same expensive or inappropriate tool.

scenes.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
scenes.narration: Model Context Protocol, or MCP, provides a standardized way for AI applications to interact with external capabilities. Look at the agent on the left, the MCP client in the middle, and the MCP server on the right. The agent asks for the status of order twelve-thousand-three-hundred-forty-five. Its client sends a structured JSON-RPC request to the MCP server, which exposes tools, resources and reusable prompts. The order-status tool then queries an external PostgreSQL orders database and returns a structured result indicating that the order has shipped. The response travels back through the MCP client to the agent. The slide's security banner is essential: MCP standardizes the interface, not the application's permissions. Authentication, authorization and data controls still need an appropriate design. The transport notes at the bottom mention local standard I/O or Streamable HTTP. Choose transport and hosting based on trust boundaries, networking and deployment requirements rather than treating MCP as an automatic secure API gateway.

scenes.title: Deploying an MCP Server on AWS
scenes.narration: Once an MCP server has been built, where should it run? The slide compares three AWS options. In the upper orange row, a lightweight stateless MCP server runs through API Gateway and AWS Lambda, optionally with CloudFront where appropriate. This can fit simple request-response workflows that don't require a persistent process. The middle blue row uses an Application Load Balancer and ECS on Fargate for a longer-running container-based server. This gives more control over process lifetime, connections and scaling. The lower cyan row illustrates an AgentCore-managed deployment option, depending on supported runtime capabilities. All three share the left-hand boundary: the client connects using HTTPS and the deployment needs an authentication mechanism, such as a supported IAM, SigV4, Cognito or other configured method. Hosting does not remove the need for input validation, scoped credentials, request limits or logging. Select a runtime based on whether the MCP workload needs long-lived connections, container features, deployment control or serverless simplicity.

scenes.title: OpenAPI and Generative AI Tool Contracts
scenes.narration: An agent tool becomes more reliable when its contract is explicit. This slide shows a small calculator API. In the first panel, an OpenAPI definition declares an add operation with two numeric parameters, a and b, and a structured response containing sum. The second panel configures a Bedrock Agent action group from that API schema. In the third panel, the agent chooses the add operation and supplies a equal to seven and b equal to five. Finally, the API returns the structured result, sum equals twelve. The orange takeaway along the bottom is the important design principle: explicit operation names, input types and response shapes reduce tool-call mistakes. A schema doesn't guarantee that an API is trustworthy or that a caller is authorized. The application still needs parameter validation, authentication, error responses and, where appropriate, approval for consequential actions. But schema-driven tool descriptions make it easier for the agent to select and invoke the correct operation.

scenes.title: Humans in the Loop
scenes.narration: This slide shows why some agent outcomes should be reviewed by a person before they are acted on. On the top row, a customer complains about being charged twice and requests a refund. A generative AI model drafts a response, but a risk or uncertainty check decides that the matter deserves human review. The reviewer can approve or edit the response before the organization sends it to the customer. That is an intervention point, not merely a quality score after the fact. Follow the lower cyan loop: the customer rates the reply, Lambda processes a feedback event, DynamoDB stores the outcome and supporting context, and the team analyses feedback to refine prompts, policies or future models. The important distinction is between human approval for a high-risk individual action and aggregate feedback for longer-term improvement. A positive rating shouldn't bypass refund permissions or erase the requirement to verify account facts. Human oversight is most useful when criteria, responsibilities and escalation paths are clear.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Business
scenes.narration: The last slide in this batch introduces Amazon Q Business as an enterprise-oriented generative AI assistant. The employee asks it to summarize the approved travel policy. The central service accesses permitted enterprise content, such as policies, internal documents and connected knowledge sources. Follow the arrow to the grounded response on the right, which includes citations back to the relevant travel-policy and expense documents. The lower panel also shows optional authorized actions, such as submitting a time-off request through a configured integration. That distinction matters: answering from a document and taking a business action have different authorization requirements. Amazon Q Business is designed to respect appropriate enterprise identity and access settings for connected content, but administrators must configure those controls correctly. The example demonstrates what a trustworthy workplace assistant should do: retrieve the relevant approved source, provide a readable answer with evidence and perform only actions explicitly permitted for that user.
